title: Kentucky driver’s licenses
summary: How Kentucky’s graduated licensing works, where licenses are issued, REAL ID, renewals, and the penalties for driving without a valid license.

body.text: Anyone who drives on a Kentucky road needs a valid license or permit. Drivers who start before age 18 earn full privileges in three steps, and licenses are issued by the Kentucky Transportation Cabinet.
The three steps for new drivers

items: Instruction permit. A person who is at least 15 may apply with a parent or guardian’s signature and must pass written and vision tests. A permit holder may drive only with a licensed driver who is at least 21 in the front passenger seat.

Intermediate license. A driver who is at least 16 and has held the permit for 180 days may take the road test. A parent or guardian must certify 60 hours of supervised practice, including 10 at night.
Full license. The Transportation Cabinet requires the driver to be at least 17, to have held the intermediate license for 180 days, and to have completed an approved driver education course.

body.text: Until age 18, permit and intermediate license holders may not drive between midnight and 6 a.m. without good cause, and may not carry more than one unrelated passenger under age 20. A violation of these rules, or a moving violation that carries points, adds at least 180 days before the next step.
A new adult driver aged 18 to 20 must hold a permit for 180 days, and one who is 21 or older for 30 days.
Where licenses are issued and renewed

Applications are handled at Transportation Cabinet Driver Licensing Regional Offices, and the Kentucky State Police give the written and road tests. A license is renewed every eight years in the driver’s birth month, or every four years if the driver chooses. The Cabinet requires a vision screening at renewal. A licensed driver who moves to Kentucky must apply for a Kentucky license within 30 days of becoming a resident.
REAL ID or standard license

A REAL ID, which state law calls a voluntary travel ID, meets federal identification standards and is accepted for boarding domestic flights. A standard license is valid for driving but does not meet those standards. A REAL ID must be requested in person.
Driving without a license

Driving without having obtained a license, or while a license is suspended or revoked, is a Class B misdemeanor, punishable by up to 90 days in jail and a fine of up to $250. A driver who simply was not carrying a valid license may show it in court, and the judge may dismiss the charge.
Driving while a license is suspended for driving under the influence is punished more severely. A first offense brings an added six-month suspension, and repeat offenses can be felonies.

sources.label: Kentucky Transportation Cabinet: Graduated Driver Licensing Program

title: Kentucky vehicle registration
summary: Who must register a vehicle in Kentucky, where and when to do it, what to bring, how title transfers work, and the penalties for not complying.

body.text: A motor vehicle must be registered with a county clerk before it is driven on a Kentucky road, and it must stay insured. A person who buys a vehicle, or brings one into Kentucky from another state, has 15 days to apply for registration.
Where to register and what to bring

An individual registers with the county clerk in the county where he or she lives. Title and registration are normally handled in the same visit. For a vehicle bought from a private seller, the Transportation Cabinet lists these items:

items: The title, signed over to the buyer.
Proof of Kentucky insurance issued within the past 45 days.
Proof of identity, such as a Kentucky driver’s license or ID card.
Payment for fees and any taxes due.

body.text: A vehicle brought in from another state must first be inspected, with its title papers, by a certified inspector through the sheriff’s office in the county where the title application will be filed.
Renewing each year

Vehicles weighing 10,000 pounds or less, including motorcycles, are registered on a schedule based on the owner’s birth month. Registration must be renewed every year during that month, at the clerk’s office or on the Transportation Cabinet’s website, and it expires on the last day of the birth month. The state sends a notice at least 45 days ahead, but not receiving the notice is no defense to a registration charge. The registration receipt for a car or truck must be kept in the vehicle, and the plate must be displayed on the rear.
Buying or selling a vehicle

In a private sale, the seller signs the assignment on the back of the title. The Transportation Cabinet requires that signature to be notarized. The seller keeps the license plate, which may be moved to another vehicle of the same class. The buyer takes the signed title and proof of insurance to the county clerk, and the transfer must be started within 15 days. If the buyer does not complete it, the seller may file an affidavit with the clerk in the seller’s home county stating that the vehicle was transferred.
Penalties

Driving a vehicle that is not registered, or whose registration has expired, is classed as a violation, which carries a fine of up to $250. Driving without the required insurance is more serious. The owner and the driver each face a fine of $500 to $1,000, up to 90 days in jail, or both, and the vehicle’s registration is revoked.
Registration and title fees change from time to time, and several county clerk fees are set to change on January 1, 2027. The county clerk can confirm current amounts.

title: Abandoned vehicles
summary: When a vehicle counts as abandoned in Kentucky, who can have it towed, the notice owners get, towing liens and sales, and how to report one.

body.text: Kentucky law presumes that a vehicle left on a public road for three days in a row has been abandoned. It can be towed, and the towing company can hold it, and eventually sell it, to cover its charges.
Vehicles left on public roads

On a county road or city street, a vehicle left for three consecutive days is presumed abandoned. Abandoning a vehicle there is punishable by a fine of $25 to $100 or 10 to 30 days in jail. The public authority in charge of the road must have a usable vehicle towed and may dispose of an unusable one right away.

On a state highway, a motor vehicle left on the right-of-way for three consecutive days is presumed abandoned, and the Kentucky State Police may order it towed. A disabled vehicle may not stay on the shoulder of a state-maintained highway for 24 hours or more.
Vehicles on private property

The owner or attendant of a private parking lot may have an unauthorized vehicle towed if signs state that the lot is private and that unauthorized vehicles will be towed at the vehicle owner’s expense. The towing company must notify local law enforcement within two hours after the tow. Cities and counties may adopt their own parking and impoundment ordinances, and local rules vary.
Notice, storage charges and sale

When police have a vehicle removed from a highway, the agency must mail the owner a notice saying where the vehicle is, that towing and storage charges must be paid, and that it may be sold if not claimed within 60 days.

The towing company must also send certified mail to the owner and any lienholder, meaning a lender with a claim recorded on the title, within 10 days. A company that follows the notice rules has a lien, a legal right to hold the vehicle until its reasonable charges are paid. If the charges remain unpaid after 45 days, the vehicle may be sold after another certified notice sent 10 days before the sale.

Some belongings are not covered by the lien and must be released on request within 45 days of the tow, including prescription medicine, medical supplies, child car seats, school materials and personal documents.
A vehicle impounded by a city or county under its own ordinance can become the local government’s property 45 days after certified notice if no one claims it.
How to report one
A vehicle that appears abandoned on a city street or county road can be reported to local police or the sheriff’s office, and one on a state highway to the Kentucky State Police.

title: Personal injury protection (no-fault) insurance
summary: How Kentucky’s no-fault auto insurance works: what basic benefits pay, who is covered, limits on lawsuits, rejecting no-fault, and key deadlines.

body.text: Kentucky is a no-fault state for motor vehicle injuries. Auto policies include personal injury protection, which state law calls basic reparation benefits. It pays an injured person’s medical bills and lost income, up to $10,000, no matter who caused the crash.
What it covers and who is covered

Basic benefits pay for economic loss from an injury: reasonable medical expenses, lost income, the cost of replacing services the injured person can no longer perform, and, after a death, funeral costs and survivors’ losses. The total is capped at $10,000 per person per accident. Since July 15, 2026, lost income and replacement services are payable at up to $500 a week, up from $200. Benefits do not pay for pain and suffering. Insurers must offer added coverage on request.

The insurer of the vehicle a person was riding in normally pays, and a pedestrian is paid by the insurer of the vehicle that struck him or her. Motorcycles are different. Coverage is optional, and a rider or passenger receives no basic benefits unless it was purchased.
Limits on lawsuits and rejecting no-fault

In exchange for these benefits, the right to sue the at-fault driver is limited. An injured person cannot recover from that driver the losses that basic benefits cover. A claim for pain and suffering is allowed only if medical expenses exceed $1,000, or the injury involves a broken bone, permanent disfigurement, permanent injury, permanent loss of a bodily function or death.

A person may reject these limits by filing a rejection form with the Kentucky Department of Insurance before an accident happens. The rejection stays in effect until it is revoked in writing. Someone who rejects keeps the full right to sue and can be sued without the thresholds, but cannot collect basic benefits unless that coverage is bought back.
Required coverage

Every owner must carry liability insurance of at least $25,000 for injury to one person, $50,000 for all injuries in one accident and $25,000 for property damage, or a single limit of $60,000. Basic benefits are required too, except on motorcycles. Owning or driving a vehicle without this insurance carries a fine of $500 to $1,000, up to 90 days in jail, or both.
Deadlines

If no benefits have been paid, a lawsuit for benefits must generally be filed within two years after the loss and no later than four years after the accident. If benefits have been paid, the deadline is two years after the last payment. A lawsuit against the at-fault driver must be filed within two years after the injury, the death or the last basic benefit payment, whichever is latest.

title: Credit card scams
summary: Common card fraud methods, federal limits on what a cardholder can lose, what to do right away, and the Kentucky crimes and reporting options.

body.text: Using another person’s credit or debit card, or card number, without permission is a crime in Kentucky. Federal law limits how much a cardholder can lose to fraud, but the protection is much stronger when the loss is reported quickly.
Common ways card information is stolen

items: Skimmers. A hidden device on a gas pump, ATM or store terminal copies a card’s data.
Phishing. An email, text or fake website poses as a bank or other trusted sender and asks for a card number, password or PIN.
Phone scams. A caller posing as the card company’s fraud department asks for the security code or a one-time passcode.
Card-not-present fraud. A thief uses a stolen number to shop online or by phone.

body.text: How much a cardholder can lose

For a credit card, federal law caps liability for unauthorized charges at $50, and only for charges made before the issuer is notified. If the loss is reported before the card is used, or if only the account number was stolen, the cardholder owes nothing.
Debit and ATM cards carry more risk. Under the federal rule known as Regulation E:

items: If the loss or theft is reported within two business days after the cardholder learns of it, liability is limited to $50.
If it is reported later, liability can reach $500.
If unauthorized transfers on a statement are not reported within 60 days after the statement is sent, the cardholder can lose all the money taken after that period.

body.text: What to do right away
Consumer agencies recommend these steps:

items: Report the loss or the charges to the card issuer or bank right away.
Follow up in writing and keep a copy.
Review statements and dispute any unrecognized charge.
Change online banking passwords and PINs.
If other personal information was exposed, consider a free fraud alert or credit freeze with the credit reporting agencies.

body.text: Kentucky crimes and reporting

Kentucky law makes it a crime to steal a card, to use a stolen, forged, expired or revoked card, or to pose as the cardholder to obtain money or goods. Fraudulent use is a Class B misdemeanor when the amount obtained over six months is under $500, a Class A misdemeanor from $500 up to $1,000, a Class D felony from $1,000 up to $10,000, and a Class C felony at $10,000 or more. Using a skimming device (KRS 434.675) is a Class D felony for a first offense, and phishing (KRS 434.697) is a Class D felony.
Card fraud can be reported to the issuer and to local police. Scams can also be reported to the Kentucky Attorney General’s office online and to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

title: Caution in charitable giving
summary: How to check a charity before giving, Kentucky’s rules for paid fundraisers, warning signs of a fake charity, and the basics of tax deductions.

body.text: Kentucky law regulates people who are paid to raise money for charities, and it treats deceptive charity appeals as unlawful trade practices. Donors still need to check a charity for themselves before giving.
Rules for paid fundraisers and charities

A professional solicitor is a person or company paid to ask for donations on a charity’s behalf. Before working in Kentucky, a professional solicitor must register with the Attorney General, post a $25,000 bond and undergo a background check.

When asking for a donation, a professional solicitor must disclose its registered name, that it is being paid, the charity it represents and how the money will be used. On request, it must say what percentage of the money raised the charity will receive.
Charities that file a federal Form 990 and solicit in Kentucky must file a copy with the Attorney General. Religious organizations raising money for religious purposes are among those exempt.
How to check before giving

items: Ask for the charity’s full name, address and phone number, whether the caller is a paid fundraiser, and how much of the gift reaches the charity.
Look for the charity and the fundraiser on the Attorney General’s lists of registered organizations and solicitors.
Use the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search tool to see whether gifts to the group are deductible.
Ask for written information, including a financial statement.

body.text: Warning signs and reporting

items: Pressure to give immediately.
A name or logo that closely copies a well-known charity.
A request for cash, gift cards or a wire transfer, or an offer to send a courier to pick up the gift.
A bill for a pledge that was never made.
Refusal to send written material or financial details.

body.text: It is unlawful to claim to raise money for a charity without its written permission, to use a name similar enough to another charity’s to mislead donors, or to send misleading caller ID information. Knowingly violating the registration or disclosure rules is a Class D felony.

A donor who paid a suspected scam by card can ask the issuer to dispute the charge. The Attorney General’s office takes scam reports online and by hotline, and the Federal Trade Commission takes them at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Tax deduction basics

Only gifts to qualified organizations are deductible, and gifts made directly to an individual are not. In general, a donor must itemize to claim a charitable gift. Beginning with tax year 2026, the IRS says taxpayers who do not itemize may deduct up to $1,000 in cash gifts to certain qualified organizations, or $2,000 on a joint return. A gift of $250 or more requires a written acknowledgment from the charity.

title: Minimum wage and overtime
summary: The minimum wage in Kentucky, rules for tipped workers, when overtime is owed, who is exempt, the seventh-day rule, and how to file a wage claim.

body.text: The minimum wage in Kentucky is $7.25 an hour, the same as the federal rate. Most covered employees must also be paid one and one-half times their hourly rate for hours worked over 40 in a week.
Minimum wage and tipped workers
Kentucky’s minimum wage statute is tied to the federal rate. If the federal rate rises above the state rate, the state rate rises to match on the same date.

A tipped employee is one who regularly receives more than $30 a month in tips. An employer may pay the lower federal cash wage, currently $2.13 an hour, only if wages plus tips equal at least the minimum wage each week, as shown by the employer’s records.
An employer may not require workers to hand over their tips. A tip pool may not include salaried employees, managers or supervisors.
Overtime and the seventh-day rule

Overtime is owed at one and one-half times the employee’s hourly rate for each hour over 40 in a workweek. The Education and Labor Cabinet states that an employee covered by the overtime law may not be given compensatory time off instead.

Kentucky also has a separate seventh-day rule. An employee who works all seven days of a workweek must be paid time and a half for the seventh day. The rule does not apply if the employee was not permitted to work more than 40 hours that week, and it does not cover supervisors.
Who is not covered
Workers excluded from Kentucky’s minimum wage and overtime rules include:

items: Agricultural workers.
People employed in a genuine executive, administrative, supervisory or professional role, and outside salespeople.
Babysitters working in the employer’s home, and certain companions for sick or elderly people.
Newspaper carriers.
Employees of retail, service, hotel and restaurant businesses with average annual sales under $95,000.

body.text: The state overtime statute also leaves out employees of retail stores, restaurants, hotels and motels. Federal law has its own coverage rules and may still require overtime for some of these workers.
Filing a wage complaint
The Division of Wages and Hours in the Kentucky Education and Labor Cabinet enforces these laws and accepts complaints online or on a paper form.

A worker may also sue. An employer that underpays is liable for the unpaid wages plus an equal amount in liquidated damages, costs and reasonable attorney’s fees, though a court may reduce the extra damages if the employer acted in good faith. An agreement to work for less than the legal wage is not a defense. A claim under the state wage laws must be brought within three years after it arises. Federal wage claims have separate deadlines.

sources.label: Kentucky Education and Labor Cabinet: Wages and Hours

title: Voting in Kentucky
summary: Who can register to vote in Kentucky, the photo ID rule, early and absentee voting, polling hours, and restoring voting rights after a felony.

body.text: A United States citizen who lives in Kentucky and will be 18 by the next general election may register to vote. Voters must show photo identification and may vote early in person, on election day or, in limited cases, by mail.
Registering

To register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, a Kentucky resident for at least 28 days before the election, and at least 18 by the next general election. A 17-year-old who will be 18 by then may register and vote in the primary.

Registration closes on the fourth Tuesday before each primary and general election. To vote in a party’s primary, a voter must have been registered with that party by December 31 before the primary. People can register and check their status at govote.ky.gov, by mail, or at the county clerk’s office.
Photo ID

Voters must show a document with their name and photograph issued by the United States, the Commonwealth of Kentucky, the military, a college or university, or a Kentucky city or county government. A standard state ID card is free for a person without a driver’s license who will be 18 by the next regular election.

A voter without that ID may still vote by signing an affirmation that gives a reason, such as lack of transportation, a lost ID, disability or illness. Since a 2026 amendment, the voter must also show another card with the voter’s name and photograph, or an approved county-issued ID card.
When and how to vote

items: Election day. Polls are open from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. local time. Anyone in line at 6 p.m. may vote.

Early voting. Any qualified voter may vote in person, with no excuse needed, on the Thursday, Friday and Saturday before election day. Voters with a listed excuse may vote in person during the six business days before that.

Mail-in absentee voting. This is limited to voters with a qualifying reason, such as age, disability, illness or military service. Requests go through an online portal that opens 45 days and closes 14 days before the election. The county clerk must receive the ballot by the time polls close.

body.text: Voting after a felony conviction

The Kentucky Constitution takes away the right to vote on conviction of a felony and allows it to be restored by executive pardon. Under an executive order issued in December 2019, the right is restored automatically to people who have completed their sentences for most Kentucky state felonies. The order excludes treason, bribery in an election and listed violent offenses, and it does not cover federal or out-of-state convictions. People who are not covered may apply individually through the state’s Civil Rights Restoration website.

title: Dying without a will in Kentucky
summary: Who inherits when a Kentucky resident dies without a will, the surviving spouse’s rights, property outside probate, and small estate options.

body.text: A person who dies without a valid will dies “intestate,” and Kentucky statutes decide who inherits. The General Assembly rewrote these rules effective July 15, 2026, putting the surviving spouse first in line. Earlier deaths may be governed by the former rules.
Who inherits
Real estate now passes in this order:

items: Surviving spouse. The spouse takes everything if the person left no descendants, or if all of the person’s descendants are also the spouse’s descendants and the spouse has no other descendants. The spouse takes one-half if the person left a descendant who is not the spouse’s, or if the spouse has a descendant who is not the deceased person’s.
Children. Whatever does not go to a spouse goes to the children, with the descendants of a deceased child taking that child’s share.
Parents, then brothers and sisters and their descendants.
Grandparents, then aunts and uncles and their descendants, then stepchildren.
The state, if none of these relatives survive.

body.text: Personal property, such as money and vehicles, goes to the same people in the same shares after funeral expenses, administration costs and debts are paid.
Other rights of a surviving spouse

The surviving spouse also has the interest that older statutes call dower or curtesy. It includes a life interest in one-third of real estate the deceased spouse owned during the marriage but not at death, unless that right was given up, and an outright one-half of the surplus personal property. Under the 2026 law, that calculation counts certain assets that pass outside probate and credits what the spouse already received from them.
A surviving spouse, or the children if there is no spouse, may also ask the District Court to set apart up to $30,000 in personal property or money as an exemption.
Property that passes outside probate

Property held jointly with a right of survivorship, payable-on-death and transfer-on-death accounts, and assets with a named beneficiary generally pass directly to the surviving owner or beneficiary, not through the estate.
Administrators and small estates

Someone must apply to the District Court to be appointed administrator, the person who collects property, pays debts and distributes the rest. The court prefers the surviving spouse, then the others entitled to inherit. If no relative applies within 60 days of the death, the court may appoint a creditor or another person.

A full administration is not always required. The court may dispense with it when the $30,000 exemption, alone or with preferred claims the spouse or children have paid, equals or exceeds the estate’s assets. It may also do so when the estate owes no debts and all beneficiaries agree in writing, after notice to creditors is advertised.

title: Power of attorney
summary: What a power of attorney does in Kentucky, how to sign one, the agent’s duties, how it ends, and why health care decisions need a separate document.

body.text: A power of attorney is a written document in which one person, the principal, gives another person, the agent, authority to handle property and financial matters. In Kentucky these documents are governed by the Uniform Power of Attorney Act, KRS Chapter 457.
Durable powers, signing and effective date
“Durable” means the document keeps working if the principal becomes unable to manage property or business affairs. A Kentucky power of attorney is durable unless it says otherwise.

The principal must sign the document, or direct another person to sign in the principal’s conscious presence. The statute does not require witnesses. A signature acknowledged before a notary public is presumed genuine, and banks and others may rely on that presumption.
A power of attorney takes effect when signed unless it names a later date or event, such as the principal’s incapacity. The document may name a person to decide when that event has occurred.
The agent’s duties
Whatever the document says, an agent who accepts the role must:

items: Act according to the principal’s reasonable expectations if they are known, and otherwise in the principal’s best interest.
Act in good faith.
Act only within the authority the document grants.

body.text: Unless the document provides otherwise, the agent must also act loyally, avoid conflicts of interest, use reasonable care, and keep a record of all receipts, payments and transactions. An agent who violates these rules must restore the value of the principal’s property. The District Court can review an agent’s conduct.
How it ends

A power of attorney ends when the principal dies or revokes it, when its purpose is accomplished, or when a court appoints a guardian or conservator for the principal’s estate, unless the court orders otherwise. An agent’s authority also ends if a divorce or legal separation action is filed between the agent and the principal, unless the document says otherwise.
Health care decisions and misuse

Medical decisions are handled in a separate document. Under the Kentucky Living Will Directive Act, an adult who can make health care decisions may sign a living will directive that names a health care surrogate and gives instructions about life-prolonging treatment. It must be written, dated, signed, and either witnessed by two adults or notarized.

A power of attorney does not make it legal for an agent to take the principal’s property for personal use, which can be prosecuted as theft. Knowingly exploiting an adult who cannot manage his or her own resources because of a mental or physical condition is a Class C felony if the loss exceeds $300. Suspected exploitation of such an adult must be reported to the Cabinet for Health and Family Services.
